destination.title: She Was Jailed Because She Was Too Poor to Pay a Fine

short47: She lost her job then her car
then her license.
Then a court took her freedom over
unpaid traffic tickets.
Can they jail you just for being broke?
In Montgomery unpaid fines only grew.
A judge signed one order:
pay fifteen hundred dollars or thirty-one days in jail.
No one asked if she could pay.
She could not and the door closed.
Her probation was run by a private
company for profit.
Forty dollars of every payment went to
them not her fines.
The more she owed the more they earned.
And decades earlier the Supreme Court had
already forbidden this.
In 1983 Bearden versus Georgia said it plainly:
you cannot be jailed just for being
too poor to pay.
The law was on her side all along.
What freed her was not the Supreme
Court but a lower-court settlement in 2014.
The rule held;
enforcing it is what failed.
Watch the full case on the channel.
Follow for more.

candidate_payload_lines: The Supreme Court of the United States answered this question a long time ago, in 1983, and the answer was no.
Of that two hundred, forty dollars never touched her actual fines.
So the one voice in the room that might have been trained to insist on the words the Constitution required, could she pay, was often the one voice that was never present.
There was no one at the table whose whole job was to say those two words out loud and make the court stop and answer them.
By 2013, that one company was working in at least a hundred Alabama courts, and roughly thirty-eight thousand people were on that company's rolls across four states.

In 2012, an Alabama circuit judge named Hub Harrington moved to stop the company's practices in a town called Harpersville, and he did not reach for gentle language when he described what he had found.
This returns us to the promise the country made, the one from 1983.
His case climbed all the way to the Supreme Court, and in the spring of 1983 the Court ruled in his favor.
It did not say the state can never make you pay a dime.
And that is the line the order against Harriet Cleveland walked straight across, because no one asked.
Cleveland's case never reached the Supreme Court at all.
It came from an ordinary lawsuit in a lower court, and from a settlement, announced in late 2014, in the case that carried her name.
The terms of that settlement read like the rule from 1983 being written out a second time, by hand, because the first time had not been enough.
A settlement, in the year 2014, had to make a city promise to stop doing the precise thing the Supreme Court had declared unconstitutional in 1983.
In March of 2015, the Southern Poverty Law Center sued the probation company under a federal racketeering statute.
You write the check, you go home, you never think about it again.
In that courtroom, on that morning, no one reached for it.
It simply never walked into the room where she was standing.

lines.text: In 2012 an Alabama judge described how courts in his own state collected fines from people too poor to pay. He called it a judicially sanctioned extortion racket.
source_lines: In 2012, an Alabama circuit judge named Hub Harrington moved to stop the company's practices in a town called Harpersville, and he did not reach for gentle language when he described what he had found. He called it a judicially sanctioned extortion racket.

lines.text: People who could not pay were put on probation, run not by the county but by a private company, in business to make a profit.
source_lines: She was placed on probation, and her probation was not run by the county. It was run by a private company, in business to make a profit.

lines.text: The model has a name. Offender funded probation. The person being punished pays for the machinery of their own punishment, and the company skims a fee.
source_lines: It is called offender-funded probation, and the premise is exactly as blunt as it sounds. The person being punished is made to pay for the machinery of their own punishment.
The company collects the debt, and skims a fee for the service of collecting it.

lines.text: By 2013 that one company was working in at least a hundred Alabama courts, and roughly thirty-eight thousand people were on its rolls across four states.
source_lines: By 2013, that one company was working in at least a hundred Alabama courts, and roughly thirty-eight thousand people were on that company's rolls across four states.

lines.text: That judge stopped it in one town. The practice went on next door, in a hundred courtrooms where nobody used a word like that.
source_lines: One judge, in one hearing, put the word extortion into the permanent record. The practice went on in the towns next door.

lines.text: The rule that says a court cannot jail you for being too poor to pay was written for a man who could not read.
source_lines: He had a ninth-grade education, he could not read, and with no work and no income, he could not pay the balance.

lines.text: He pleaded guilty to burglary and theft. The court fined him five hundred dollars and ordered restitution on a schedule. He borrowed money to make the first payments.
source_lines: He pleaded guilty to burglary and theft, and the court sentenced him to a five hundred dollar fine and two hundred and fifty dollars in restitution, on a schedule
He borrowed the money to make the first two hundred.

lines.text: Then he was laid off. He could not pay the balance, and Georgia revoked his probation and sent him to prison for the shortfall.
source_lines: Georgia revoked his probation and sent him to prison for the shortfall.

lines.text: In 1983 the Supreme Court ruled in his favor. What the Constitution forbids is jailing a person for the sole reason that they cannot pay, without ever asking whether they could.
source_lines: His case climbed all the way to the Supreme Court, and in the spring of 1983 the Court ruled in his favor.
jailing a person for the sole reason that they cannot pay, without ever stopping to ask whether they could.

lines.text: That answer still stands. Thirty years later, in a Montgomery courtroom, nobody in the room said it out loud.
source_lines: It simply never walked into the room where she was standing.
